title: WHEN SUBMISSION DOES NOT MEAN PARTICIPATING IN SOMEONE’S FOOLISHNESS
paragraphs: WHEN SUBMISSION DOES NOT MEAN PARTICIPATING IN SOMEONE’S FOOLISHNESS
Sometimes the most submissive thing you can do is refuse to help someone destroy what God entrusted to them.
And sometimes the sentence, “You’re supposed to submit,” is not coming from a heart that wants to honor Scripture.
It is coming from someone who wants Scripture to stop you from questioning their foolishness.
That difference matters.
Because there are people reading this who have spent years wondering whether honoring God means remaining silent while somebody they love keeps making reckless decisions.
A wife watches her husband gamble with the family’s stability.
A husband watches his wife repeatedly make choices that are tearing their home apart.
An adult child is pressured to cooperate with a parent’s dishonesty because “the Bible says honor your father and mother.”
A church member sees something deeply wrong but is told that questioning leadership is rebellion.
An employee is ordered to participate in something deceptive and is reminded that Christians should respect authority.
A believer watches somebody walking straight toward disaster and thinks...
“If I say something, am I being rebellious?”
“If I refuse, am I dishonoring them?”
“If I set a boundary, am I failing God?”
“If I expose what is happening, does that mean I am not submissive?”
Maybe nobody ever told you this clearly:
Biblical submission is not permission for another human being to recruit your conscience into their foolishness.
Read that again.
Because somewhere along the way, some Christians learned a counterfeit version of submission that sounds holy until you examine what it produces.
Silence.
Fear.
Enabling.
Manipulation.
Spiritual intimidation.
And sometimes participation in actual sin.
But biblical submission was never designed to replace obedience to God.
The Greek language of the New Testament makes this worth slowing down for.
Before Paul speaks specifically about marriage in Ephesians 5, he writes:
— Ephesians 5:21
The phrase may be translated, “submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.”

The word ὑποτασσόμενοι, from ὑποτάσσω, carries the idea of placing or ordering oneself under. In its Christian context, submission involves humility, proper order, and willing recognition of God-given relationships.
But notice what governs the entire sentence.
“ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ.”
“In the fear,” or reverence, “of Christ.”
Christ is still Lord.
Not your husband.
Not your wife.
Not your parents.
Not your pastor.
Not your boss.
Not your government.
Not the person who knows enough Bible vocabulary to make disobedience sound spiritual.
Human authority in Scripture is real.
But human authority is never God.
And that means there comes a moment when submission to human authority and obedience to divine authority can collide.
The apostles encountered exactly that.
They were commanded to stop preaching Jesus.
Their response was not arrogant.
It was not anarchic.
It was not a declaration that authority no longer mattered.
It was a recognition that earthly authority had reached a boundary it had no right to cross.
Peter and the apostles answered:
“Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ Θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις.”
“We must obey God rather than men.”
— Acts 5:29
Notice the word δεῖ.
“We must.”
There was something higher than compliance.
There was obedience to God.
That means biblical submission can never legitimately require biblical disobedience.
And Scripture gives us an extraordinary picture of this principle in a woman who refused to participate in her husband’s foolishness.
Her name was Abigail.
Her husband was Nabal.
And even his name becomes significant in the biblical story.
When Abigail later explains the situation to David, she says:
“Let not my lord regard this worthless fellow, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him.”
— 1 Samuel 25:25
The Hebrew noun נָבָל, nābāl, is associated with foolishness or senselessness—not merely low intelligence, but the kind of morally disordered foolishness Scripture repeatedly condemns.
And Nabal was behaving exactly that way.
David and his men had been a protective presence around Nabal’s shepherds. When David requested provisions, Nabal responded with contempt.
“Who is David?”
He insulted him.
Dismissed him.
Humiliated him.
And David became furious.
Furious enough to prepare for bloodshed.
Now imagine Abigail hearing what her husband had done.
She could have said:
“He is my husband.”
“I have to support his decision.”
“It isn’t my place to interfere.”
“Submission means standing behind him.”
“If his foolishness destroys this household, at least nobody can accuse me of disrespecting him.”
But Abigail understood something that generations of believers desperately need to recover.
You do not honor somebody by helping their foolishness reach its full destructive potential.
So Abigail acted.
She gathered food.
She went toward David.
She intervened.
She pleaded.
She used wisdom.
She humbled herself without surrendering discernment.
She showed extraordinary respect while simultaneously refusing to allow Nabal’s foolish decision to determine the fate of their household.
And then something breathtaking happened.
David did not condemn her.
He blessed God for sending her.
He told her:

“Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me! Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand!”
Do you see it?
Abigail’s intervention prevented disaster.
But there is another layer.
She did not only save her household from Nabal’s foolishness.
God used her to save David from David’s foolishness too.
Everybody in that story needed somebody willing to interrupt destruction.
Nabal needed interruption.
David needed interruption.
The household needed intervention.
And Abigail possessed enough courage to become the interruption.
That is biblical wisdom.
There are moments when love says yes.
There are moments when humility stays quiet.
There are moments when wisdom patiently yields.
But there are also moments when love stands in the doorway and says:
“No. I will not help you do this.”
Not because love disappeared.
Because love finally became courageous.
This is where the subject becomes uncomfortable.
Some people do not actually want submission.
They want immunity from accountability.
They want agreement without discernment.
They want loyalty without truth.
They want authority without responsibility.
And when questioned, they reach for spiritual language.
“Respect me.”
“Honor me.”
“Submit.”
“Don’t touch the Lord’s anointed.”
“God put me over you.”
But authority that comes from God remains accountable to God.
A husband cannot demand that his wife sin because Ephesians 5 speaks about submission.
In the same passage, the husband is commanded to love his wife “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).
That is cruciform leadership.
Self-giving.
Sacrificial.
Christ-centered.
A Christian husband does not receive Ephesians 5 as a weapon with which to enlarge himself.
He receives a cross.
Neither can a wife demand her husband cooperate with wrongdoing in the name of marital unity.
Neither can parents turn the command to honor father and mother into permission to command their children to violate God.
Neither can pastors turn biblical church leadership into personal sovereignty.
Neither can governments make themselves God.
Neither can employers purchase your conscience with a paycheck.
The principle remains:
Christ is Lord.
This does not mean Christians get to call every inconvenience, disagreement, or decision they dislike “foolishness.”
That would be another form of rebellion dressed in religious clothing.
Biblical submission sometimes means yielding when you would personally choose differently.
Not every disagreement is sin.
Not every imperfect decision justifies resistance.
Not every mistake requires confrontation.
Not every preference deserves a theological argument.
Sometimes maturity means saying, “That would not have been my choice, but I can honor this decision.”

There is an enormous difference between disagreeing with someone's judgment and being asked to participate in sin, deception, abuse, serious irresponsibility, or conduct that violates a clear command of God.
That distinction requires humility.
Because your feelings are not Scripture either.
Your instincts are not infallible.
Your trauma is not infallible.
Your spouse is not infallible.
Your pastor is not infallible.
And neither are you.
Jesus is Lord.
Scripture is our authority.
So before calling resistance “obedience to God,” ask yourself whether God has actually spoken clearly about the matter or whether you simply want God to endorse your preference.
That question can expose both manipulation and rebellion.
Sometimes the controlling person needs repentance.
Sometimes the supposedly “submissive” person needs courage.
And sometimes the person convinced everyone else is foolish needs enough humility to discover that the fool in the room might be staring back from the mirror.
The Gospel confronts all of us.
That is what makes Christianity different from self-help dressed in Bible verses.
Jesus did not come merely to validate us.
He came to save us.
He exposes pride.
He exposes control.
He exposes cowardice.
He exposes manipulation.
He exposes rebellion.
He exposes the secret places where we have learned to call fear “peace” and enabling “love.”
Then He offers something astonishing.
Grace.
Maybe you participated in foolishness because you were terrified of losing somebody.
Maybe you stayed quiet because you thought silence was holiness.
Maybe you knew something was wrong but allowed it because confrontation frightened you.
Maybe you have been the controlling person.
Maybe you quoted Scripture to win arguments.
Maybe you demanded loyalty when what you really needed was accountability.
Maybe you called disagreement “disrespect.”
Maybe you hurt somebody and then used spiritual language to make them feel guilty for bleeding.
If that is you, do not run from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Repentance is not humiliation.
It is the doorway home.
The cross means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
Real sinners.
Controlling sinners.
Cowardly sinners.
Proud sinners.
Fearful sinners.
Religious sinners.
Rebellious sinners.
Broken sinners.
People like us.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin did not matter.

The Gospel is God taking sin so seriously that Christ bore its judgment, then offering forgiveness so freely that repentant sinners can walk out of their graves without pretending they were never dead.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He can teach the domineering husband to wash feet instead of demanding a throne.
He can teach the fearful wife that gentleness and courage can live in the same heart.
He can teach parents to lead without controlling.
He can teach children to honor without participating in sin.
He can teach leaders that shepherding is not ownership.
He can teach wounded believers that forgiveness does not require calling evil good.
He can teach the proud to apologize.
He can teach the frightened to speak.
He can teach all of us to submit first and finally to Him.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been waiting for permission to stop helping another person destroy themselves.
Here it is—but receive it carefully.
You have permission to obey God.
You have permission to tell the truth in love.
You have permission to refuse participation in sin.
You have permission to seek wise, godly counsel.
You have permission to say, “I love you, but I cannot help you do this.”
You have permission to remain respectful without surrendering your conscience.

And when abuse, violence, coercion, exploitation, or danger is involved, biblical submission should never be twisted into an argument that you must silently remain available for harm. Seek appropriate safety, trustworthy pastoral wisdom, qualified professional help, and lawful protection when needed.
But remember Abigail.
Her courage was not loud rebellion.
It was discerning intervention.
She did not need to become foolish in order to prove she respected a fool.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody needs tonight.
You do not have to become foolish to prove that you are faithful.
Maybe this article exposed something.
Maybe you have been enabling what God has been asking you to confront.
Maybe you have been demanding “submission” when God has actually been demanding your repentance.
Maybe you have been confusing control with leadership.
Maybe you have spent years carrying guilt because someone convinced you that saying no to their wrongdoing meant saying no to God.
Bring it into the light.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only person fighting this battle.
Not because every disagreement requires confrontation, but because someday emotion may make you forget the difference between biblical submission and sinful complicity.
Not as a weapon aimed at a particular person. Share it as an invitation for all of us to examine ourselves under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Salvation is by grace, not by supporting a page.
Support Gospel work because you freely believe the work is worth supporting.
Your share may place biblical truth in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
Because one share can become somebody's interruption.
One truthful conversation can stop somebody's destruction.
One courageous “no” can protect what foolishness was about to ruin.
One humble “I was wrong” can begin rebuilding a marriage.
One confession can end years of pretending.
One encounter with the Gospel can change eternity.
And maybe the person God is calling out of foolishness today...
isn't the person you've been arguing with.
Maybe it's you.
Never confuse helping someone disobey God with loving them—sometimes grace reaches into the fire by refusing to hand them another match.
